newsitem.title: USA: US announces modifications of Boeing 737 rudders.
newsitem.headline: US announces modifications of Boeing 737 rudders.

text.p: Federal safety officials will order Boeing Co. to modify the rudder system of its popular 737 jet, two of which have been involved in still unexplained fatal crashes, Vice President Al Gore announced on Wednesday.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the changes would help prevent inadvertent rudder movement which could throw the plane into a sudden and uncontrolled roll.
Acting FAA Administrator Linda Daschle said in a statement: "We believe the steps the FAA is requiring today will make a safe airplane even safer.'
The retrofitting is to be done over three years.

Gore made the announcement at the end of a three-day international conference on aviation safety and security. He said the FAA's actions "will enhance safety, in partnership with the aviation industry."

The FAA has said rudder problems have not been found to be the cause of the crashes at Pittsburgh in 1994 and at Colorado Springs in 1991, although in both cases the 737s went down after going into sudden rolls.

Investigations by Boeing and the National Transportation Safety Board had found the 737 rudder power control could jam when subjected to unusually extreme temperatures, although the board has not yet determined the causes of either crash.
The Pittsburgh crash of a USAir jet killed 132 people and the United Airlines Colorado Springs crash killed 25.

FAA officials said 737 rudder components were to be refitted to prevent jamming and uncommanded rudder movement and a modification would be made to help a pilot control the jet in case of a sharp rudder movement, known as a hardover.

The FAA said the actions were part of its overall review, with Boeing, of the flight control system of the widely used 737. They are to be included in new 737s and to be retrofitted in the 2,700 now flying worldwide.

Boeing said tests showed that if the rudder power control did jam, the 737 could roll in one direction and possibly go out of control, but the problem had never been encountered in the some 69 million flights of the 737s flying worldwide.
Boeing vice president Chet Ekstrand said in a statement the proposed changes were "reasonable, appropriate and technically sound."

Mike Denton, chief project engineer on the 737, said Boeing and its suppliers expected to spend $120 million to $140 million on parts required by the worldwide fleet of the world's most widely used jet to comply with the directive.
The Air Line Pilots Association praised the FAA and Boeing and called for other changes including the addition of rudder pedal parameters to "black box" the flight data recorders.
The pilot's union said the added parameters would help accident investigators determine what rudder actions the pilot had taken prior to a crash.

Boeing also said it plans to add a parameter to the 737's "black box" that will measure force applied to the rudder pedal. And it plans new training procedures to help pilots learn how to recover from unusual events caused by bad weather or malfunctions during flight.

Gore also announced that the Defence Department would make mapping data available to civil aviation which when used with advanced navigation systems could reduce or eliminate so-called "controlled flight into terrain."
He said crashes into mountains or in landings occur when pilots cannot reconcile their instrument positions with their actual positions relative to changing terrain.
Gore cited the crashes into mountains of an American Airlines jet in Columbia and a military jet in Croatia, one of whose passengers was Commerce Secretary Ron Brown.

He also announced a two-year FAA trial of "free flight" air navigation in Hawaii and Alaska that would allow pilots, using the latest navigational aids, including satellites, to choose the best and most direct route to their destinations.
Gore said the Hawaii and Alaska experiment would later help improve air traffic throughout the United States.
